docs.title: Medicaid's January 2027 Double Deadline
docs.text:
An Implementation Guide For Work Requirements And Six-Month Renewals

A member who works 90 hours a month can still lose Medicaid in 2027 if the proof doesn't reach the state in time. Most 2023–24 unwinding losses happened that way. From January 1, 2027, expansion adults must meet a new community engagement requirement and renew their coverage every six months instead of once a year. Every extra renewal is another form that can arrive late. In my view, the states that keep eligible people covered will be the ones that check the data they already hold before they ask anyone for proof.

Read the requirements See the documentation checklist

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
What changed Signed on July 4, 2025, H.R. 1 links Medicaid for many expansion adults to 80 hours a month of work, school or community service. It also halves the time between eligibility checks.

What breaks Roughly 24 million people lost Medicaid in the 2023–24 unwinding. For between 66% and 74% of them, the cause was a late form or an unanswered notice rather than a finding that they no longer qualified. Each new rule adds forms to that same process.

What it costs CMS itself expects about 2.3 million people to lose coverage in 2027 because of the work requirement. Some will be people who did the hours and couldn't prove it. Each state decides how many, through the data it checks first and the plain wording of the notices it sends to members.

docs.title: Regulatory Change Log
docs.text:
• July 4, 2025NewH.R. 1 is signed into law. It creates the community engagement requirement and moves expansion adults to six-month renewals.
  • March 6, 2026GuidanceCMS sends states a State Medicaid Director Letter on six-month renewals, including the two ways to transition.
  • June 1, 2026NewCMS publishes interim final rule CMS-2454-IFC on community engagement.
  • July 31, 2026DeadlineThe comment period on the interim final rule closes.
  • July 1 to September 1, 2026DeadlineAdvance outreach notices fall due, with each state's date set by its look-back period.
  • October 29, 2026RulingA federal court strikes down part of the medically frail definition in the interim final rule.
  • January 1, 2027EffectiveWork requirements and six-month renewals take effect.
  • December 31, 2028DeadlineEvery good-faith exemption that delays a state's start runs out.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
• Ex Parte Renewal - Renewal based on data the state already holds, with nothing asked of the member.
  • Expansion Adults - Adults eligible for Medicaid through the Affordable Care Act's expansion group.
  • Interim Final Rule - A rule that takes effect before public comment closes. The agency can revise it afterwards.
  • Look-Back Period - The months before an application that a state reviews for compliance.
  • Procedural Disenrollment - Loss of coverage over paperwork, such as a form never returned, with no finding of ineligibility.

docs.title: Who It Applies To
docs.text:
Work requirements Non-pregnant adults aged 19 to 64 in the Medicaid expansion group or certain section 1115 demonstrations, as long as they aren't enrolled in or entitled to Medicare. CMS puts the number of affected states at 43, plus D.C.

Six-month renewals Adults covered through the expansion, whether under the state plan or a waiver for the whole expansion group. Children, parents and pregnant or postpartum people stay on 12-month renewals. American Indian and Alaska Native enrollees do too.

docs.title: What Members Must Show
docs.text:
Qualifying activities A member needs 80 hours a month of work, community service or a work program, or half-time enrollment in school. Hours from different activities can be added together.

Income instead of hours Earning at least the federal minimum wage times 80 hours also counts. In 2026, that's $580 a month.

When it's checked Applicants have to show one to three months of compliance before the month they apply, and the state picks the number. Enrolled members must meet the requirement in at least one month of every eligibility period, and states are free to verify more frequently.

docs.title: Who Is Exempt
docs.text:
The interim final rule requires states to exclude these groups:

  • Former Foster Youth - who turned 18 on or after January 1, 2023.
  • American Indians And Alaska Natives - regardless of income or activity.
  • Parents And Caregivers - of a child aged 13 or under, or of a person with a disability.
  • Disabled Veterans - with a total disability rating from the VA.
  • Medically Frail Individuals - including people with serious mental illness, substance use disorder, or physical, intellectual or developmental disabilities.
  • Members Already Meeting Other Program Rules - people meeting TANF work requirements, or SNAP household members not subject to SNAP work rules.
  • People In Treatment - in a drug or alcohol treatment and rehabilitation program.
  • Incarcerated Individuals - in a public institution.
  • Pregnant And Postpartum Individuals - through the end of the postpartum period.

A federal court struck down part of the medically frail definition on October 29, 2026. Part 2 covers what changed.

States may also grant short-term hardship exceptions. They cover inpatient care, federally declared disasters, travel for medical care and counties where unemployment is at least 8% or 1.5 times the national rate, whichever is lower.

docs.title: The Renewal Rules
docs.text:
Automatic renewal first A state has to attempt renewal with the data already on file. If the data falls short, the member gets a prepopulated form and at least 30 days to send it back.

Two ways to make the switch CMS's State Medicaid Director Letter of March 6, 2026 gives states a choice. They can keep each member's current renewal date and start six-month periods at the next renewal. The alternative is to pull renewals forward from January 2027. No period can start before January 1, 2027 or run shorter than six months, and any member whose 12-month period is cut short must be told in writing.

Mixed households One household can now hold members on different renewal cycles. If a six-month renewal surfaces information about another member of the household, the state has to handle it as a change in circumstances.

docs.title: Where The Two Deadlines Collide
docs.text: Pulling renewals forward risks a renewal surge in January 2027, the month work checks begin. Caseworkers would take on two new processes in the same weeks, and members would receive a heavier stack of notices. CMS has warned that processing backlogs could expose a state to compliance action. Keeping existing renewal dates is the safer choice, because it spreads the work across the year.

docs.title: What Changes In Eligibility Systems
docs.text:
• Eligibility Rules - New logic sorts members into subject and exempt and decides which months count. It has to run at application, at renewal and at every extra check a state adds.
  • Data Matching - Automated checks against payroll, claims and agency data. A member who already complies should never see a request.
  • Notices - Templates for advance outreach, noncompliance, hardship exceptions and coverage loss, with each timing rule built into the template itself.
  • Caseworker Task Queues - Cases the data can't settle go to a queue sorted by deadline, where a 30-day window can't lapse without someone seeing it.
  • Reporting And Audit Trail - Every check, notice and decision gets logged, because any of them can come up at a fair hearing.

docs.title: Documentation Checklist
docs.text:
• Member Notices - Plain language, with the action, the deadline and the method stated before anything else.
  • Caseworker Procedures - Step-by-step guides for exemptions, hardship requests and the cases data can't settle.
  • System Release Notes - Staff get a short note with every system change, covering what moved and what they now do differently.
  • Version History - Keep a record of when each notice and procedure changed. At a fair hearing, one of the first questions will be which version the member was sent.
  • Review Sign-Off - Policy, legal and QA should all read a notice before it goes out. If one of them hasn't, it isn't ready to send.

docs.title: Release Notes Template
docs.text: Field What To Write What's Changing One sentence on the change. Who It Affects Members, caseworkers or both. Effective Date The date the change applies. What You Do Now The new steps, numbered. Where To Get Help The contact or resource for questions.

docs.title: Rewriting A Member Notice
docs.text:
An illustrative example. It isn't taken from any state's notice.

Before

Pursuant to federal requirements, your continued eligibility for medical assistance is contingent upon verification of compliance with community engagement requirements. Failure to furnish acceptable documentation within the prescribed period may result in termination of benefits.

After

Action needed by [date]: Tell us about your work, school or volunteering

To keep your Medicaid, we need to know you spent at least 80 hours in [month] working, studying, volunteering or in a job program. We couldn't confirm this from the records we have. You can upload pay slips or a school letter at [website], call [number], or return the enclosed form. If something stops you from meeting this requirement, such as a health condition or caring for a child, tell us. You may not need to meet it at all.

docs.title: How States Must Verify
docs.text:
Data before paperwork Before a state asks a member for anything, it has to check what it already holds. The rule lists payroll data, 12 months of Medicaid claims and encounter data, records from other state and local agencies, federal data through CMS's data services hub and the state's own eligibility files.

Self-declaration has a limit Medical frailty can rest on a member's own statement only through January 2028, and the first renewal after that has to include supporting documents.

Health plans can help, but not decide Managed care plans are allowed to contact members and point out the ones who may qualify for an exemption, but the call on eligibility or compliance is the state's alone.

docs.title: Notices And The 30-Day Window
docs.text:
Advance outreach States owe members a first notice no later than three months, plus the length of the look-back period, ahead of the start date. A state with a one-month look-back and a January 1, 2027 start had to send it by September 1, 2026. With a three-month look-back, the cutoff moved up to July 1, 2026.

Noncompliance notice A state that can't verify compliance sends a notice. From five days after the notice date, the member has 30 calendar days to show compliance or an exemption. Enrolled members stay covered throughout.

Before coverage ends No one loses coverage until the state has looked for another Medicaid pathway they qualify under. The member also gets a written notice with fair hearing rights, along with an explanation of how losing Medicaid may affect Marketplace premium tax credits.
